a-manifesto-mindset.title: Agile Manifesto values and twelve principles; agile as mindset, values, principles and practices; agile as an umbrella term; two strategies to become agile
a-manifesto-mindset.notes: The Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) values individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan - the items on the right have value, the items on the left are valued more. Twelve principles (paraphrased): (1) highest priority is customer satisfaction through early and continuous delivery of valuable software; (2) welcome changing requirements, even late, for the customer's competitive advantage; (3) deliver working software frequently, weeks rather than months, preferring the shorter timescale; (4) business people and developers work together daily; (5) build projects around motivated individuals - give environment and support and trust them; (6) face-to-face conversation is the most efficient and effective way to convey information to and within a team; (7) working software is the primary measure of progress; (8) sustainable development - sponsors, developers and users can maintain a constant pace indefinitely; (9) continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility; (10) simplicity - maximising the amount of work not done - is essential; (11) the best architectures, requirements and designs emerge from self-organising teams; (12) at regular intervals the team reflects on how to become more effective and adjusts. Principles now apply well beyond software. Figure 2-3 (inspired by Ahmed Sidky): agile is a mindset defined by 4 values, guided by 12 principles and manifested through many practices; practitioners select practices based on need; many techniques predate the Manifesto by years or decades. Figure 2-4: agile is a blanket term for approaches, techniques, frameworks, methods or practices fulfilling the values and principles (Scrum, XP, FDD, DSDM, AUP, Crystal, ScrumBan); agile and the Kanban Method are shown as subsets of lean, sharing lean concepts such as focus on value, small batch sizes and elimination of waste. The guide uses the term 'approach'. Two strategies: (1) adopt a formal agile approach designed and proven to work, and learn it well before tailoring - premature, haphazard tailoring limits benefits; (2) change project practices to fit the context and make progress on a core value or principle (timeboxes, iterative feature refinement, splitting a large project into releases) even if not part of formal organisational practice. The goal is not agile for its own sake but a continuous flow of value to customers and better business outcomes.

a-lean-kanban-uncertainty.title: Lean and the Kanban Method; uncertainty, risk and the Stacey-inspired complexity model
a-lean-kanban-uncertainty.notes: Agile and the Kanban Method descend from lean thinking (a superset) and share a heritage: delivering value, respect for people, minimising waste, transparency, adapting to change, continuous improvement; teams may blend methods - the best outcome matters, not the origin. The Kanban Method is inspired by lean manufacturing and applied to knowledge work; emerged in the mid-2000s; less prescriptive and less disruptive than some agile approaches - the original 'start where you are' approach; teams can begin easily and progress to other approaches; debate continues whether it belongs to lean or agile. Uncertainty about requirements and about how to fulfil them with current knowledge and technology raises rates of change and complexity; as uncertainty increases so do the risk of rework and the need for a different approach; teams tackle high uncertainty with small increments of work they can verify and change, learning true customer requirements faster than from a static written specification. Figure 2-5 (inspired by the Stacey Complexity Model): axes - requirements uncertainty (agreement) and technical degree of uncertainty; low/low = simple, where linear approaches work well; moving outward = complicated, then complex, where adaptive approaches work well; high/high = chaos, fundamentally risky. Clear, stable requirements and clear technical challenges are easy to plan; rising uncertainty increases changes, wasted work and rework. Iterative and incremental approaches reduce waste and rework through feedback, using very short feedback loops, frequent process adaptation, reprioritisation, regularly updated plans and frequent delivery. Tip example: the Boston 'Big Dig' moved an elevated highway underground - high agreement on requirements and apparently low uncertainty until surprises emerged; with little opportunity for interim deliverables or prototypes, a predictive life cycle is likely; assess both requirements and means of delivery. Agile approaches suit new or novel tools, techniques, materials or domains, research and development, high change, unclear requirements or high risk, or goals hard to describe; small tested increments explore uncertainty cheaply in product specification (right product?), production capability (can it be built this way?) and process suitability (is this an effective way to work?). Limits: when both technology and requirements uncertainty are very high the project becomes chaotic and one variable must be contained to make it reliably possible.

a-life-cycle-types.title: Life cycle selection: predictive, iterative, incremental and agile characteristics; planning in every life cycle; iteration-based vs flow-based agile; suitability filters
a-life-cycle-types.notes: Four life cycles: predictive (bulk of planning up front, then executing in a single pass; sequential); iterative (feedback on unfinished work to improve and modify it); incremental (finished deliverables the customer may use immediately); agile (both iterative and incremental, refining work items and delivering frequently). Terminology: 'predictive' chosen over plan-driven, waterfall or serial to align with the PMBOK Guide. Table 3-1 (verified order): requirements - predictive fixed; iterative, incremental and agile dynamic. Activities - predictive performed once for the entire project; iterative repeated until correct; incremental performed once for a given increment; agile repeated until correct. Delivery - predictive single delivery; iterative single delivery; incremental frequent smaller deliveries; agile frequent small deliveries. Goal - predictive manage cost; iterative correctness of solution; incremental speed; agile customer value via frequent deliveries and feedback. All projects have these characteristics; inherent characteristics decide the best fit. Figure 3-1 presents the continuum as a square: frequency of delivery (low to high) vs degree of change (low to high) - predictive low/low, incremental high delivery, iterative high change, agile high/high. Predictive exploits known, proven things; iterative improves partially finished work via feedback; incremental gives usable finished deliverables; agile combines both, giving early feedback, customer visibility, confidence and control and possibly earlier ROI by delivering highest-value work first. Predictive characteristics: high certainty on firm requirements, stable team, low risk; serial execution with detailed plans; succeeds when change is restricted; constraints from detailed early plans manage risk and cost; M&C controls changes to scope, schedule, budget; departmentally efficient serial work usually delivers business value only at the end; unexpected changes, disagreements or difficult technology cause unanticipated costs. Sidebar 'planning is always there': every life cycle plans - the difference is how much and when; predictive plans as much as possible up front (plan drives the work, detailed requirements, delivery estimates, comprehensive procurement); iterative plans prototypes whose outputs modify early plans; incremental plans successive subsets; agile plans and replans as information comes from frequent deliveries. Iterative: successive prototypes or proofs of concept, each yielding stakeholder feedback and insight that is fed back by repeating activities; timeboxing iterations of a few weeks; useful when complexity is high, change is frequent or stakeholders differ on the desired final product; may take longer because optimised for learning rather than speed (Figure 3-3: analyse, design, prototype, refine cycles before build, test, deliver). Incremental: optimised for speed of delivery - customers accept a subset; plan initial deliverables and start the first as soon as possible (some agile projects deliver within days; others 1 to several weeks); deviations from the original vision are manageable because value comes sooner; e.g., builders finishing one floor completely (fixtures, paint) so the customer approves style before the rest - reducing rework and dissatisfaction; completeness is subjective - a prototype then a minimum viable product (MVP) to a subset of customers whose feedback shapes the final feature. Tips: when requirements seem to change daily, a prototype the business approves encourages feedback; use a proof of concept with evaluation criteria to explore a new business service. Agile: requirements are expected to change; incremental delivery uncovers hidden or misunderstood requirements. Iteration-based agile: equal-duration timeboxes delivering completed, working, tested features; the team swarms on the most important feature then the next, never doing all requirements then all analysis. Flow-based agile: features pulled from the backlog by capacity, workflow defined as task-board columns with work-in-progress (WIP) limits per column; each feature may take a different time; small WIP surfaces issues early; the team and stakeholders choose the schedule for planning, reviews and retrospectives. Agile life cycles fulfil the Manifesto principles - early, continuous delivery and a functional valuable increment as the primary measure of progress. Agile suitability filters: assessment models score project and organisational factors for fit or risk (synthesised in APG Appendix X3).

a-hybrid-tailoring.title: Hybrid life cycles (agile then predictive, combined, largely predictive with agile parts, largely agile with predictive parts, fit-for-purpose, transition strategy); mixing approaches; project factors that influence tailoring
a-hybrid-tailoring.notes: A hybrid approach combines predictive, iterative, incremental and/or agile elements; one approach is not required for the whole project. Agile development followed by a predictive rollout (Figure 3-6) - uncertain, complex development then a defined, repeatable rollout, perhaps by a different team (e.g., a new high-tech product then rollout and training to thousands of users). Case: a pharmaceutical company ran drug trials in an agile way but the FDA approval had to stay as a separate final phase because any change requires re-approval; integrating it iteratively failed, but quick-start guides and testing protocols shortened approval. Combined agile and predictive used simultaneously (Figure 3-7) - e.g., a team transitioning with short iterations, daily standups and retrospectives but still predictive upfront estimation, work assignment and progress tracking; neither fully agile nor predictive - hybrid. Largely predictive with agile components (Figure 3-8) - e.g., an engineering firm building a routine facility with a new roofing material runs small installation trials on the ground to learn the best method early. Largely agile with a predictive component (Figure 3-9) - when an element is non-negotiable or not executable with agile, e.g., integrating an external vendor component delivered once by a vendor that will not collaborate incrementally. Fit-for-purpose hybrids based on risk - e.g., a campus construction project completing some buildings earlier (incremental) while each building is predictive. Goal: produce business value in the best way for the environment; ask 'How can we be most successful?' - need feedback as value is produced? use increments; need to manage risk while exploring ideas? use iterations or agile; if intermediate value can't be delivered agile may not help - agile for the sake of agile is not the goal. Case: a government credit insurance system replacement - mostly agile with continual business input, but a premium-rate calculation defined in a 200-page OECD specification was coded by a separate team in a largely predictive way, coordinating only on inputs and outputs. Hybrid as a transition strategy: organisations can't switch overnight; add iterative techniques for learning and alignment, later incremental techniques for faster value and ROI; start with a less risky project of medium-to-low uncertainty before more complex ones. Mixing agile approaches: teams rarely use just one; frameworks are not customised to the team, so teams tailor; a common blend is Scrum (product backlog, product owner, scrum master, cross-functional development team, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective) + a kanban board (visualise flow, expose impediments, manage WIP limits) + XP-inspired engineering practices (story cards, continuous integration, refactoring, automated testing, test-driven development) - a synergistic result. Table 3-2 (factor -> tailoring option): demand pattern steady or sporadic -> use a cadence (regular timebox) for demos, retrospectives and taking new work, or flow-based agile with a cadence for flexibility; rate of process improvement needed given team experience -> retrospect more often and select improvements; flow interrupted by delays or impediments -> make work visible with kanban boards and experiment with WIP limits; poor quality of increments -> test-driven development practices (mistake-proofing); more than one team needed -> learn agile program management or formal scaling frameworks, then craft a fitting approach; team inexperienced with agile -> train in the agile mindset and principles, then a workshop on the chosen approach (e.g., Scrum or Kanban).
